carries-its-story.q: How does a workbook keep knowing what it is after you rename the file to anything?
options: Its file extension is locked so a rename can never alter the type.
The browser caches the original name and restores it on open.
A hidden magic header in the first bytes declares its true type.
It carries an internal marker block that describes what it is.
carries-its-story.explain: Identity lives inside the file as a marker block, so a rename never reaches it.

carries-its-story.q: What is the filename's one humble remaining job during a library scan?
options: It narrows the pile so the scan need not crack open every file.
It is the only way the tool decides which files are workbooks.
It stores the workbook's embedded source for fast retrieval later.
It records the author and timestamp of the most recent change.
carries-its-story.explain: The extension narrows the haystack for economy, but the marker is still the needle.

carries-its-story.q: Why can a workbook carry its own source while still looking like one finished thing?
options: The browser compiles the source on load and discards the original text.
The readable source folds into a second inert block the browser ignores.
The source is fetched from a server the moment someone unpacks the file.
A binary section stores the recipe in a sealed, unreadable container.
carries-its-story.explain: The human-written source rides along in a second inert block the browser leaves untouched.

carries-its-story.q: How does a workbook project keep its history instead of scattering it?
options: It uploads every revision to a vendor dashboard's activity log.
It saves periodic snapshots in a separate folder beside the files.
Its working space is a version-controlled repository kept inside it.
It records only the final published version and discards the rest.
carries-its-story.explain: The project's working space is a version-controlled repo, so history travels with it.

carries-its-story.q: What makes the author of each recorded change trustworthy rather than a typed label?
options: The name is verified against a central company directory at publish time.
Each change requires a fresh password confirming the author manually.
The author field is locked once written and can never be edited again.
A real cryptographic identity backs the name and survives a wipe.
carries-its-story.explain: Authorship rests on a portable cryptographic identity, not a name typed into a field.

the-one-language.q: What is the central claim this lesson makes about what an agent writes?
options: The material underneath is just readable plain text you can check.
The agent hides its real plan in a private machine language.
Only experts trained on the tooling can decode what was written.
The running result is all there is; nothing underlies it.
the-one-language.explain: The whole idea is that the layer you and the agent stand on is just readable.

the-one-language.q: What trade do the two usual ways of writing software's story force on you?
options: You must pick a vendor's format and stay locked inside its tools.
You get prose or structure in one place, never both together.
You choose between speed and accuracy when the machine parses it.
You sacrifice readability for a smaller file that loads faster.
the-one-language.explain: Pretty prose is meaningless to a machine; tidy structure has no room for human thought.

the-one-language.q: Where did the org convention come from?
options: It was invented fresh for this project to unify its layers.
It is a proprietary dialect owned by a single vendor.
It is a roughly twenty-year-old convention for plain-text notes.
It is a rebranding of HTML extended to describe meaning.
the-one-language.explain: Org is a ~20-year-old open convention for notes, to-dos, and schedules, not newly invented.

the-one-language.q: What does org's readability actually give you about agent drift?
options: It prevents an agent from ever repeating or contradicting itself.
It compresses the text so contradictions cannot fit in the file.
It locks the document so only the host can change a line.
It makes drift catchable, since a checker can walk it and notice.
the-one-language.explain: Org doesn't prevent drift; being machine-readable makes the drift catchable instead of hidden.

the-one-language.q: Why does learning to read one format let you read every corner of a project?
options: The same org grammar shows up in intent, manuals, deploys, and plans.
A translator converts each part into your preferred file format.
Every part is rewritten into prose whenever you open it.
Each layer uses its own dialect that the reader auto-detects.
the-one-language.explain: The same readable grammar appears everywhere, so you learn it once and read it all.

coming-alive.q: What changes when a workbook on your laptop comes alive?
options: The file is rewritten into a server-specific binary format.
Nothing about the file changes; the thing it stands on does.
The browser injects new code so the page can run on its own.
Its source is stripped out to make room for live state.
coming-alive.explain: The same byte-for-byte file comes alive because of what it stands on, not any file change.

coming-alive.q: What is the Nexus in this system?
options: A file format you hand around like any other workbook.
A cloud-only subscription metered per request you make.
The engine — a place you run that workbooks are set down on.
A converter that exports a workbook into a deployable app.
coming-alive.explain: The Nexus is the load-bearing engine, a place you stand on, not a file you carry.

coming-alive.q: How do the three words Nexus, dock, and the Dock relate?
options: They are three separate systems you configure independently.
They are older names for one deprecated deployment step.
They describe three competing engines you pick between.
One motion seen three ways: the place, the act, the doorway.
coming-alive.explain: Nexus is the place, to dock is the act, the Dock is the doorway between them.

coming-alive.q: Which trio of lights switches on when you dock a workbook?
options: Isolated, stateful, and agentic.
Compiled, encrypted, and signed.
Cached, indexed, and replicated.
Public, billed, and metered.
coming-alive.explain: Docking flips three lights at once: isolated, stateful, and agentic.

coming-alive.q: Why can one ordinary machine carry many workbooks at once?
options: Each workbook is paused unless someone is actively viewing it.
The BEAM juggles huge numbers of tiny isolated processes.
Workbooks share one process so overhead stays near zero.
The engine rents extra virtual machines per workbook by the second.
coming-alive.explain: The BEAM was built to juggle vast numbers of lightweight, isolated processes.

why-a-sandbox.q: What are the two things that actually go wrong with an agent doing real work?
options: It runs too slowly and it forgets earlier parts of the task.
It writes buggy code and it picks the wrong AI model.
It reaches where it shouldn't, and it gets hijacked through the work.
It costs too much per run and it crashes the host machine.
why-a-sandbox.explain: The two nightmares are excess reach and prompt injection riding in on the work.

why-a-sandbox.q: How does a sandbox differ from putting a guard in front of your secrets?
options: It checks permissions twice instead of once before each action.
It encrypts the secrets so a guard can't read them if fooled.
It logs every access so a fooled guard can be caught later.
It builds a room that doesn't contain the secrets at all.
why-a-sandbox.explain: There's no door to guard because the secrets were never in the agent's room.

why-a-sandbox.q: What does the phrase "grant the verb, keep the noun" mean here?
options: The agent gets the ability to act, never the dangerous thing itself.
The agent is given verbs to log but nouns to execute directly.
The host renames secrets so the agent can't recognize them.
The agent may read keys but is forbidden from sending them.
why-a-sandbox.explain: The agent gets the ability to sign or fetch, never the key or network that's dangerous.

why-a-sandbox.q: What's the difference between "forbidden" and "doesn't exist" for a capability?
options: Forbidden means slower access; doesn't exist means no access at all.
Forbidden has a check that can fail; doesn't exist has nothing to check.
Forbidden applies to data; doesn't exist applies only to networks.
Forbidden is temporary; doesn't exist means revoked for this run.
why-a-sandbox.explain: A forbidden capability still exists and is checked; an absent one has nothing to check.

why-a-sandbox.q: Which wall in the sandbox is described as the most thoroughly tested?
options: The memory limit, pinned down by a dedicated automated suite.
The file-system wall, verified by checks after a past leak.
The network wall, pinned by checks after an early leak was caught.
The shell wall, proven by repeated red-team attempts.
why-a-sandbox.explain: The network wall is the most tested, pinned by checks after an early version leaked.

safe-powers.q: What is the narrower, more honest claim this lesson actually makes?
options: Every dangerous power is silently filtered before it can run.
The powers are removed entirely so nothing risky remains.
A smarter guard catches every misuse before it happens.
You hand powers over deliberately and can take any back.
safe-powers.explain: The claim is deliberate, named, revocable grants, not danger magically erased.

safe-powers.q: What happens when a workbook reaches for a power it was never granted?
options: It fails to even start, because it asked for a tool never wired in.
It gets a quiet "no" and continues with reduced abilities.
It pauses and prompts the host to grant the power on demand.
It logs the attempt and silently skips that one action.
safe-powers.explain: An ungranted power doesn't exist, so the workbook fails to start rather than being denied.

safe-powers.q: What does the minimal profile actually include?
options: Only a disk and nothing else, a fully sealed scratch space.
Disk, commands, storage, a queue, plus secrets and brokered sockets.
Everything except the ability to call a language model.
Outbound web and browsing but no local disk or storage.
safe-powers.explain: Minimal is a working surface that also grants secrets and brokered sockets, not a sealed space.

safe-powers.q: What happens if someone names a profile that doesn't exist, like a typo?
options: It grants the network rung so the run isn't blocked.
It refuses to run until a valid profile name is supplied.
It falls closed to the pure-compute floor, disk and nothing else.
It inherits the last profile that successfully ran before it.
safe-powers.explain: Unknown profiles fall closed to the most restrictive disk-only floor, pinned by a test.

safe-powers.q: How can a workbook use a secret without ever being able to leak it?
options: The secret is encrypted inside the workbook and decrypted on use.
The workbook reads the key but is audited every time it does.
The host rotates the key fast enough that a leak goes stale.
It names and uses the secret but never reads it; the host signs.
safe-powers.explain: With secrets granted it can name and use a secret but never read it; the host holds the key.

going-live.q: Why is going live usually terrifying, according to the lesson?
options: Many separate services must all agree at once for the move to work.
The new place runs different code than your local prototype did.
Deploying always erases your data unless you back it up first.
The cloud charges unpredictable fees the moment you publish.
going-live.explain: The fear is the committee of services that must all line up, not the new place itself.

going-live.q: What is a deployment, in this system's terms?
options: A scripted sequence of steps that must run in the right order.
A short list of five decisions the engine converges reality to.
A configuration file packed with hooks and embedded commands.
A one-time export that bakes the current state into a binary.
going-live.explain: A deployment is five decisions described as an end state the engine converges to.

going-live.q: What does the validation check do before letting you go live?
options: It starts a test machine to confirm the deploy actually boots.
It rewrites the config to fix problems for you automatically.
It refuses configurations that would quietly betray you, read-only.
It flags style issues so the file reads more cleanly.
going-live.explain: The read-only check refuses lying configs, like many tenants with single-user storage.

going-live.q: What does the public /_changes endpoint serve, and how?
options: A full admin console gated behind a required login.
A live edit surface where anyone can push new commits.
The secrets and build tools, available only to authorized users.
The history feed, anonymous and read-only, newest first.
going-live.explain: /_changes is an anonymous, read-only GET serving recent changes and agent status.

going-live.q: How does moving from your laptop to production actually work?
options: You change one setting; local and cloud are values of one axis.
You rebuild the app for the cloud's different engine and runtime.
You migrate through a separate deploy pipeline and rebuild train.
You re-author the prototype into a production-grade version.
going-live.explain: Local and cloud are two values of one setting; the same engine and bytes run on both.

giving-it-abilities.q: What does an agent reach for when it needs an ability it doesn't have?
options: A plugin locked to whichever platform supplied it.
A toolkit: one packaged ability it can find, learn, and run safely.
A raw package installed onto your machine at your own risk.
A custom protocol bolted onto the agent for each new tool.
giving-it-abilities.explain: An agent reaches for a toolkit, one packaged ability bundled to be found and run safely.

giving-it-abilities.q: What three things does a toolkit bundle into one object?
options: A license, a price, and a support contract.
A protocol, a server, and a registry entry.
The program, the manual, and the sandbox-shaped wrapper.
A name, an icon, and a version number.
giving-it-abilities.explain: A toolkit ships code, manual, and the sandbox wrapper bound together as one object.

giving-it-abilities.q: How is a toolkit's "muscle" layer built?
options: A fresh program written from scratch for every new toolkit.
A description of a program the agent interprets at run time.
A cloud service the toolkit calls out to over the network.
A real program compiled into the portable form browsers run.
giving-it-abilities.explain: The muscle is a real program brought across into the portable form that runs in browsers.

giving-it-abilities.q: Why can the manual double as the agent's instructions for the tool?
options: It is structured text precise enough to be how the tool is reached.
A separate hidden spec is generated from it for the agent to read.
The agent rewrites the loose prose into commands before each use.
The manual is compiled into the program so they never diverge.
giving-it-abilities.explain: Structured manual text is precise enough to reach the tool, so docs can't drift from it.

giving-it-abilities.q: How does the shared collection of toolkits actually grow?
options: A central team writes and approves each new toolkit in advance.
Useful things built inside workbooks get promoted into toolkits.
Vendors submit toolkits to an app store for paid distribution.
The engine auto-generates toolkits from popular agent requests.
giving-it-abilities.explain: Build something useful inside a workbook and one step promotes it into a shared toolkit.
